comment: Increasingly apartment communities are providing building-wide networks for tenants to use. My own apartment complex requires the use of this network to use sort-of wired broadband at all, which provides excellent Internet bandwidth but impairs the performance of or often outright breaks local networking. That is, a failure in Charter's equipment can prevent and has prevented my laptop from talking to my desktop, and I'm not legally allowed to fix it by connecting to the Internet through my own network--the best I can do is connect up to two devices through an Ethernet switch. Charter won't sell normal service to me without permission from the property owners, which I haven't gotten despite complaining for more than six months; and their contract somehow forbids me from buying service from AT&T. Charter's network doesn't support inbound connections at all, so if you want to host a Minecraft game for remote friends you're out of luck. Charter's network uses a weak password users cannot change for initial sign-on, then uses easily spoofed MAC addresses to authenticate connections to the network from that device. A moderately over-achieving 14-year-old can commit online crimes and make it look like they're happening from my apartment, and there's nothing I can do to stop them without disconnecting all of my devices from the connection permanently. And that only works if they can't guess the password to just authorize their own device. Routing local traffic through the ISP's equipment also raises privacy and civil rights concerns--is my LAN traffic now also subject to wiretap orders? Is Charter gathering information about the types of computers and local network services I use? Does Charter have the technical ability to attempt to connect to those services which ought to be exposed only to members of my household? As ISPs push these "community WiFi" solutions on additional apartment communities, problems like these will plague more and more people in America's largest population centers and will become harder and harder for consumers who cannot or should not buy their own real estate to escape. These agreements to allow Charter's or any other ISP's own managed network to be the exclusive sort-of-wired broadband for a property are an end-run around FCC regulations requiring cable subscribers be allowed to attach their own equipment to the cable network, they inextricably tie Internet providers to apartments, they severely limit what consumers can do with their own local networks, and this non-legal-expert isn't even sure how this is allowed under the Sherman Antitrust Act. Not only do I think these agreements should be outright banned, but services like this raise questions about how we define the term 'Internet access.' Users forced to use these connections cannot be full Internet participants and limited service like this should not be sold as equivalent to or better than residential wired broadband.

comment: An "authorized signer" can be added to a credit card account without the knowledge of the person being added. (No credit report is pulled on that person.) The credit card account is a part of the authorized signer's credit report - it shows as an authorized signer. If the credit card is delinquent this negatively affects the authorized signer - even though they never signed anything and had no knowledge of being added to the account. The authorized signer was required to pay a higher interest rate because of this account on their credit report - everything else on the credit report was stellar. A complaint was filed but it was stated that there was no violation of the FCRA. This seems unfair. Nothing should appear on anyone's credit report unless the consumer has authorized it.

comment: Hello. Thank you for the opportunity to submit comments regarding to "Made in USA" claims. I was fooled for many years by product makers' words regarding their products being "Made in USA" or "Product of USA." One of the best examples is when the packaging states "Made in USA," but after purchasing, the truth comes out on, say, the operating instructions. Then and only then can a consumer learn the truth.....i.e., the item was not made in the United States, rather it only was distributed from the company's headquarters in the United States. If I remember correctly, my first experience with this was with a Ryobi electric sander at Home Depot. There, the products are displayed without boxes/instruction sheets. I believe that the description of the sander I was looking at had "Made in USA" either on the actual tool or on Home Depot's "description tag" that shows model number, etc. It was only after they brought one down from the shelf and I took it home and opened the box that I learned the real story about the sander from the instructions packed inside. Made in China. Distributed from their warehouse in the USA. Since that time, I've been careful to either contact the company for clarification or open the packaging right in the store to inspect the operating instructions and any other paperwork contained within the packaging. (This is where you learn that you might as well, just stop trying to find anything made in the USA.) It should be required (I've seen it on some things) that the packaging, both inside a box and out, state the truth. If the item was assembled in China, but distributed from US warehouses, it should be clearly stated in a place where the potential buyer doesn't have to tear open packaging and root through the internal contents for the truth. The store owners don't like you to do that, however, I do it anyhow. Sad but true, usually there is no choice but to buy the Chinese made product because there just aren't that many things made in the US. At least if we knew up front what we were buying we could make an informed decision whether to continue with the purchase. Thank you again for the opportunity to comment. Jan Darvas Sacramento, CA .

comment: Loot boxes, hands down, are a form of digital gambling. Most gaming companies, which employee these loot boxes, do so without the customer in mind. After spending $60+ for a video game, which is usually under-developed, they hide many of the game's best items behind a "paywall". Meaning, they deliver a half-polished video which includes minimal content, then users can and are forced pay even more money to gamble on gaining more items to make the game more fun. Many times, users will end up spending an exponential amount of money, which ends up shadowing the initial cost of the game. For many years, games were released in a fully polished form, allowing users to aquire all items in the game without the need to pay extra for various items, content, etc. Sometimes, games would release expansions, which cost extra money normally, and are essentially another game which extends the original. This practice has seemed to fade over time and companies such as Electronic Arts (EA) will do as I described above, release a half built product and make users pay a large amount of money extra to fully enjoy the game. They, and others, have adopted very anti-consumer type practices. The even larger issue has to do with non-adults (>18 years old). Many of these youths will acquire their parents, guardian's, etc. credit cards and purchase these loot boxes. With hopes of winning an item they want, just to give them a temporary dopamine hit. If they do not win the item they want, they can fall into a pattern of continually purchasing loot boxes, racking up a hefty bill for whomever is paying for it. Then there is the aspect of adults who purchase the game expecting to have all the content available to obtain (through working in the game and being rewarded). With loot boxes, many of us save up for these games since they cost a lot of money, but are then forced to buy loot boxes, or something similar, to actually enjoy the product we already spent a lot of our hard working money on. It would be the same as buying a new cell phone, only, the cell phone did not include a charger, headphones, etc. then we have to spend $5 here and there to "roll" with the hopes of eventually getting that charger. Which is needed to actually enjoy and use the phone.

comment: Loot boxes can enhance gameplay when they are used as a fun way to get cosmetic items that do not have any impact on in game power. However, they are often used as a stealth pay wall: 1) Game play is often altered so that progression is tied to loot box luck rather than in game accomplishments (earning tokens to open loot boxes rather than actual items, for example) 2) Most have no mercy rule (guaranteed top prize after a set number of attempts to offset really bad luck...important since the odds of getting desired items are often lower than 1%). 3) From my experience in free to play games that have loot boxes, the top players end up gambling thousands of dollars to make sure they have the best stuff. Those who dont pay sometimes get lucky, but usually dont stand a chance against those that do. 4) Games often use tactics like always on PvP or tying important items for progression to PvP. In short, what could be a fun mechanic is often being abused to hold your progress ransom to dumb luck.

comment: In considering the value of COPAs for patients and the healthcare system, please consider the academic research on Certificate of Need regulations, which is another state-based regulatory approach intended to control healthcare prices and improve quality. Like COPA laws, some state regulators support CON with the belief that government regulation reduces unnecessary duplication of healthcare resources and controls healthcare costs. I began studying CON regulations several years ago with a favorable attitude, because I believed that concentrating complex surgical operations at a smaller number of high-volume hospitals would build greater expertise and therefore better outcomes for patients. In 2009, I published a study that compared the experience of 7 states that dropped CON for open heart surgery and cardiac catheterization to states that maintained the regulations over the period 1989 to 2002 (Ho et. al., Health Services Research 2009). We found that states that dropped CON for cardiac care witnessed a 14% increase in the number of hospitals performing open heart surgery and a 12% rise in the number of hospitals providing cardiac catheterization relative to states that kept CON. As the total number of procedures was spread out over more facilities, the average volume of open heart surgeries and cardiac caths dropped roughly 30% in states that dropped CON rules, relative to states that maintained them. Nevertheless, there was no difference in mortality for cardiac care patients in states that dropped CON versus those that kept the regulations. In states that dropped CON, patients were able to choose from more facilities, without any increased risk of mortality. I published a study in 2012 that compared the cost consequences for the same 7 states that dropped CON regulations for cardiac care versus states that maintained the regulations (Ho and Ku-Goto, Medicare Care Research and Review 2012). We found that states that dropped CON experienced lower costs per patient for CABG but not for percutaneous coronary intervention. Average Medicare reimbursement was lower for both procedures in states that dropped CON. The cost savings from removing CON regulations slightly exceed the total fixed costs of new CABG facilities that entered after deregulation. Taken together these two studies imply that CON regulations are not justified in terms of either improving quality or controlling cost growth. These findings are supported by more recent studies that have concluded that removing CON for home health would have negligible systemwide effects on health care costs and quality (Polsky et. al. Journal of Public Economics 2014), and that CON laws have no statistically significant effect on allcause mortality (Bailey, Health Services Research 2018). Well-intentioned state CON regulations have not improved patient outcomes or lowered costs for patients. Healthy market competition amongst hospitals is a better strategy for improving patient welfare. Bailey J., The Effect of Certificate of Need Laws on AllCause Mortality, Health Services Research, 2018; 53(1): 49-62. Ho V, Ku-Goto MH, Jollis JG. Certificate of Need (CON) for cardiac care: controversy over the contributions of CON. Health Services Research, 2009; 44(2 Pt 1): 483-500. Ho V, Ku-Goto MH. State deregulation and medicare costs for acute cardiac care. Medical Care Research and Review, 2013; 70(2): 185-205. Polsky D, David G, Yang J, Kinosian B, Werner RM, Journal of Public Economics, 2014; 110:1-14.

comment: Full comments in attached filing -- along with White Paper outlining privacy regulations and actions regarding technology. We appreciate the opportunity to submit this comment to the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) as it evaluates the direction of competition and consumer protection enforcement and policy in the 21st Century. Throughout these hearings, some participants wrongly suggested that the FTC should revise or otherwise supplement its regulation of the technology industry, particularly in the areas of privacy, data security, and competition. When evaluating these recommendations, we urge the Commission to reject these proposed changes and recognize the robust regulatory frameworks that apply to the technology industry today. NetChoice is a trade association of leading e-commerce and online companies promoting the value, convenience, and choice of internet business models. Our mission is to make the internet safe for free enterprise and for free expression. We work to promote the integrity and availability of the global internet and are significantly engaged in privacy issues in the states, in Washington, and in international internet governance organizations. With this comment, we submit a white paper that describes the myriad ways in which the technology industry is highly regulated across a myriad of issue areas, including in the competition and consumer protection contexts. Specifically, we describe the extensive regulatory frameworks that govern how technology companies interact with consumers, manage content, and conduct themselves in the market. We begin with a high level overview of the laws, regulations, and other requirements that apply to technology companies and are enforced by federal agencies, state officials, and private litigants across the country. We then provide a more detailed outline of these authorities, case examples, and other information that will aid the Commission in assessing the existing regulatory landscape. Our analysis provides details on the many substantive areas that regulations of technology companies address. In the attached, first we identify the federal and state consumer protection, privacy, and data security laws, regulations, self-regulatory programs, and other authorities that govern how technology companies interact with consumers. For example, we describe how the FTC uses its Section 5 authority to bring enforcement actions against technology companies for alleged unfair and deceptive practices, including in the areas of privacy and data security, and how states attorneys general bring similar law enforcement actions. We explain how federal agencies issue and enforce regulations of digital practices based on sectoral laws, and outline more general consumer protection authorities that govern, among other things, advertising, adware and spyware, online disclosures, and endorsements. Second, we identify federal laws and regulations that impose liability or otherwise put regulatory pressure on technology companies with respect to the content on their platforms. For example, we describe how federal copyright laws impose direct and secondary liability on platforms for allegedly infringing copyright or facilitating the infringement of copyright on their platforms. We also describe how platforms are subject to robust notice and takedown requirements, and how recent legal developments have expanded technology companies potential exposure to liability for user-generated content on their platforms. Third, we outline the federal and state laws, regulations, and guidelines that restrict how technology companies conduct themselves in the market. For example, we describe how federal agencies regulate antitrust in the U.S. through laws such as the Sherman Antitrust Act, the FTC Act, and the Clayton Act, among others, and how state officials supplement this authority by bringing enforcement actions under their own versions of federal antitrust and unfair competition laws. We also discuss how private litigants provide enforcement efforts by bringing private antitrust cases against companies in the technology industry, and how patent laws have placed additional constraints on technology companies practices. In sum, we urge the Commission to recognize the comprehensive legal framework that currently protects consumers and other businesses while allowing the Internet to grow and power the economy. If, despite the panoply of laws, rules, and enforcements discussed in the attached paper, the FTC decides to pursue new regulations, those new regulations must solve a problem and specific harm to consumers or other businesses, and avoid causing collateral damage that will impact the U.S.s longstanding position as the leader in technology innovation.

comment: Efforts to improve the value of care for the people of the region have increased exponentially with the creation of the physician led Clinical Council under the COPA agreement. I am a physician in private practice and I have worked at multiple Ballad and former MSHA facilities for nearly 14 years. One of the best products of the merger was the Clinical Council. The Clinical Council is engaging physicians in the region in setting high standards of care and eliminating unnecessary costs. Physicians in the community are advocating for their patients and partnering with Ballad Health to improve quality and safety in Ballad facilities, and this is happening on a scale that did not exist previously. I can honestly say Ballad's commitment to quality of care is not just lip service; it seems to be true and genuine. As a physician, I feel that Ballad is hearing my concerns and my ideas on behalf of my patients, and positive change is happening as a result. Making changes to standardize and improve care across 22 facilities, involving hundreds of physicians and thousands of other care-givers takes time, but we are already witnessing the results. For example, hospital acquired infections have dramatically decreased in the past year due in large part due to the partnership between physicians of the Clinical Council and the Ballad health infection prevention team. Our hard work is paying off and we are capable of even more when we work together.

This small percentage of people are those who suffer from gambling and shopping addictions, as well as those who have not been exposed yet but are a qualified target for these practices. I care for video games, almost as much as I care for my own parents even, so I only wish that the industry as a whole can realize the mistakes they have made before it is too late. It is with all of these things in mind that I ask you to do what the industry themselves refused to do, and regulate Loot boxes please, or better yet, ban them. These practices are vile and predatory in nature and if we give them an inch, they will take a mile.

comment: I have been a practitioner and teacher of antitrust law from my graduation from Harvard Law School in 1967 to my recent retirement as a law firm partner specializing in the antitrust aspects of mergers and acquisitions. A highlight of my career was my stint from 1977-79 as an Assistant Director for General Litigation in the FTC's Bureau of Competition. The FTC that I knew, respected (and, indeed, loved) during my time there and for many years thereafter was an essentially nonpartisan institution manned to a great extent by career employees of unquestionable dedication and devotion to serving the competition mission with fairness and impartiality, and overseen by senior managers and commissioners who largely shared that public service mindset. One of the mainstays of FTC practice was the existence of the administrative law judge who managed the administrative hearing process. The ALJ's actions were, of course, subject to Commission review and the ultimate Commission decision, but the ALJ's status -- at one remove from the fray, and typically with the respect earned through years of experience at this important work -- provided both the appearance and reality of impartiality. And what can be more important than that in an adjudicatory setting? While the shortness of time allowed by the 30-day comment period allows only these brief preliminary comments, I do want to make the following points: (1) 30 days is too brief for comments on a proposal that would make such drastic changes in the administrative process at the FTC. Why such a rush? Why foreclose the opportunity for considered comments by antitrust scholars, practitioners and organizations, and for reasoned consideration by the Commission of these comments? In this election year, the truncated timing of the comment period suggests a rush to resolve this matter before a change of administrations and in the membership of the Commission. Hopefully, this result was unintended, but nonetheless the perception of an unseemly rush to change the long-established rules does not serve the Commission well. (2) A rigid time frame for the commencement of an administrative hearing is a one- size-fits-all solution for diverse situations that can better be managed by an experienced ALJ who can impartially assess the needs of a particular case, including the amount of time necessary for the respondent to have a fair opportunity to prepare its defense. This is exactly the kind of nitty gritty hands-on function that ALJs perform so well. (3) Continuing to entrust the ALJs with responsibility for pretrial motions keeps responsibility for case management centered in the hands of the FTC official with the closest and best view of the case in the pretrial and administrative trial phases, as well as some independence from the initial decision to vote out a complaint. Absent a factual showing of disabling deficiencies in this process, which has served the Commission and litigants well for many years, this long-established practice should not be abandoned. The appearance of the Commission reaching to micromanage and control pretrial proceedings marks a profound change in the administrative process. As a young antitrust lawyer, I recall marveling at the strangeness of the Commission voting out a complaint as prosecutors and then putting on judge's hats and sitting in judgment on the case that they initiated: it is useful for all of us to continue to appreciate what a curious system this is. I came to think of the time that the case was in the hands of the ALJ as a sort of cooling off period, where others could work up the facts and assess the theories and bring considered work product back for the consideration of the Commission in its adjudicatory role: why mandate Commissioner intrusion into this phase too? Respectfully submitted, Linda Blumkin

comment: My son has attended feeding therapy and occupational therapy at the Laughlin Memorial Hospital pediatric rehab group (a Ballad Health facility in Greeneville, TN) for almost 2 years. The therapists are excellent, and we've enjoyed the time we've had with them. On April 1, Laughlin switched to a new computer system, which we were notified of in advance. What we were not told (and the rehab group staff were not told, either) is that the prices would be going up at the same time. For every weekly visit for the 2 years we've been there, we have self-paid $52 for feeding therapy (since our insurance doesn't cover it), and were billed $105.60 for the OT (the amount after insurance is billed). The OT bills have regularly been incorrect, but the office manager and cashier at Laughlin have helped me get them fixed. Now, we are being charged $223 for feeding therapy (they are no longer giving us the self-pay discount on top of the increase), and $206 for OT. The insurance is not paying anything for either of these services (I'm assuming there's been a change in the contract, since deductibles, etc. have never been a factor in the amount we've paid previously). The staff at Laughlin have tried to help, but the account access they used to have has been revoked by Ballad. When I called the Ballad central billing office, I was on hold for over 10 minutes, and then told that they had no record of any charges beyond March. So, the therapy office can't give me any information, the billing office can't give me any information, but I'm still receiving bills. Our weekly charge has now tripled. We were not notified in advance of this price change, and by the time we figured out what was going on 6 weeks later, I now owe over $1600. The entire staff at Laughlin have been amazing in helping us with what they can, but their hands have also been tied by Ballad. We are now looking at other options, since we can no longer afford to use the group that my son has been with since he was 2 years old. This will, no doubt, set him back in his therapy gains, as it will require time to get used to a new therapist and new routines. This may seem like a minor inconvenience, but for children like my son who have feeding and sensory issues, and borderline autism, it is life-altering.

comment: I believe it is necessary to consider a further revision to the definition of Personal information (Question 13). First, the definition of Personal Information in 2013 revised COPPA Rule does not take a unified identifier of the devices into consideration. Sequences of data collected, such as the MAC addresses or IP addresses can tell the comparable physical presence of the user. When combined with other information collected from the user, it can generate a unified profile of the child or children using the device, which should also be regarded as personal information. Second, the behavioural data of the child using the device surfing should also be considered, which can be very identical and personal. Third, biometric data including facial and voice recognition should also be included as personal information. Forth, in an environment of peer-to-peer communication based online service, an identifier that can trace back to a certain child user either with certain behaviour or able to accept incoming information should be considered as personal information. For the Question 24, I dont think the Commission should consider a formal exception to verifiable parental consent when an operator collects an audio file with a child's voice without prior parental consent even if the audio file is collected solely as a replacement for written words, such as to perform a search or the audio file is held for a brief time and used only for that purpose. Voiceprint recognition has already been adopted by several call centres including those of financial institutions as a technology to identify the clients. Being a biometric identifier, there is a potential risk that processing such data might be misused. Even the storage of data can be attacked or hacked.

comment: The proposal to have the seller verify only the contact lens brand or manufacturer is problematic for a few reasons, most of which would be anti-competitive and ultimately result in higher prices for consumers. The crux of the issue is that some contact lenses may be similar to the prescribed brand and have the same/similar material properties, base curve, diameter and thickness but have a different brand name or manufacturer. Under this scenario, a seller would not be able to offer this 'generic' brand as it may not be explicitly requested by consumer (the customer may not know this brand is an option or the manufacturer). This provides an advantage to the established, higher priced brands despite broad similarity to alternative offerings. This is akin to restricting generic medicines in favor of only established, branded medicines - something that is not in the interest of consumers and health care costs in America. Perhaps a more sensible and consumer friendly approach would be to verify prescriptions according to material and/or base curve and diameter. Whilst not perfect, it would allow more competition in the lens market and leave it up to the consumer to decide which lenses fit according to their preference and budget (albeit there should be flexibility to change material if desired). Alternatively, an equivalency based on material used can also be established based on FDA data for various lens brands registered by the FDA. This would level the playing field instead of limiting consumer options to just a brand name. It is quite apparent that this section of the draft proposal mostly benefits the established players and eye care professionals at the expense of consumers. Furthermore, it is well known that a handful of lens manufacturers account for an outsized proportion of the contact lens market and have a vested interest in maintaining this market share. The current draft proposal only enables this further. Finally, there is an element of scare mongering by eye care professionals against alternative 'generic' brands that has not been empirically proven in other markets. Other developed countries (ie in the European Union) allow consumers with prescriptions to purchase and try regulated and approved lens brands which may be broadly similar to see what works for them, with minimal adverse effects to date (ie if it doesn't work, customers discontinue). For example, a consumer should be able to switch from a higher priced silicon hydrogel lens to a more affordable hydrogel lens if they desire without much friction or additional costs. The ability to do this has resulted in more choice, better customer service, convenience and lower prices for consumers in the EU. Perhaps this is something that should be taken into consideration in light of the changes in technology that have enabled consumers to have more choice and control over their purchasing habits.

comment: I believe that companies have a right to proprietary information. But I do not believe that this extends forever. Therefore, as long as a company warranties a product their proprietary boundaries should not be crossed. But if a company is not warranting certain parts of a product there is no proprietary boundaries being conflicted with. A consumer also has a right to be able to have a product, they purchased, fixed at a reasonable price. A company should not be able to hold a consumer hostage strictly on the issue of proprietary information. There is a balance that needs to be reached. This balance is simply once the product is no longer warrantied by the manufacturer the company's proprietary information rights are relinquished, to a major extent. The company should have to release all schematics, specification and repair information so that the consumer can make a decision on where to get their product repaired. The manufacturer and his suppliers should also have to make available all parts, specialty tools, diagrams, and other information needed to repair the consumer product. The consumer should have the right to decide where they want to have a product, that they purchased, repaired after the warranty runs out. Or if the consumer is having work on a product that does not come under the manufacturer's warranty. The manufacturer does not own this product the consumer owns this product. As stated, I believe the manufacturer has a right to their proprietary information but after a certain amount of time this proprietary information is obsolete; therefore, the consumer also has rights and I believe the consumer's rights are being dismissed. But, I believe at this time manufacturer's rights far exceed consumer rights. The manufacturers are using proprietary information as a means to make additional profits off of a product after the warranty has run its course. This is wrong. The consumer should have the right, after the warranty has run its course, to have their product repaired where they want. Under the current situation, I believe, the manufacturer is holding the consumer hostage.

comment: As a practicing ophthalmologist owning a small business, I am deeply concerned about proposals included in the Federal Trade Commission's proposed amendments to the Contact Lens Rule. While I would welcome changes to the Contact Lens Rule that prioritize patient safety, the prescription-receipt verification process and three-year record hold places an unfair burden on ophthalmology practices that are already overloaded with documentation requirements. These sort of requirements detract from patient care and are a financial hardship on small medical practices such as mine. This new burden is also unwarranted, as there is little evidence that ophthalmologists are not in compliance with the existing Contact Lens Rule. I strongly urge the FTC to withdraw its latest proposed changes to the Contact Lens Rule and focus on efforts to enhance patient safety. Thank you for your consideration.

comment: Dear Chairman Simons, I am a doctor of optometry providing primary eye health and vision care in our local community. For more than two years, my fellow eye doctors and I, and the patients and communities we serve with dedication, have faced the threat of a seriously flawed Federal Trade Commission (FTC) plan to impose massive new costs and far-reaching new requirements on all contact lens prescribing. The proposal, even in its latest form, will divert precious resources away from the care and innovation at the heart of my practice and cast public doubt on the integrity of optometrists and ophthalmologists, our para-professional staff and other employees. It should be withdrawn once again, and re-worked to put the interests of patients, doctors, and public health and safety first. I have and will continue to comply fully with the prescription release requirements of the 2003 Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act. The agencys own records and data clearly demonstrate that eye doctors across the country, in overwhelming numbers, comply as well. Instead of creating new burdens from Washington, DC impacting tens of thousands of doctors and millions of patients, please commit to a program of basic enforcement focused on outliers shown to be violating the law. What would be preferred is for this agency to do a better job of monitoring all the internet contact lens retailers which repeatedly and consistently refill outdated prescriptions, make illegal substitutions (changing brand names at will) without ever contacting the prescribing doctor. I took an oath to do not harm, internet contact lens retailers are not bound by any oath but their own greed. Its especially notable that the FTCs actions remain at odds with the policy direction being pursued by Congress and Federal agencies to prioritize the elimination of burdensome, costly and unjustified mandates in health care, especially those that are overwhelming small and mid-sized health practices on the frontlines of care. Here are active examples that I hope the agency is aware of: -Patients over Paperwork: CMS initiated this regulatory review in 2017 aimed at removing regulatory obstacles that get in the way of providers spending time with patients. -Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA): Currently, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) is considering eliminating or modifying the requirement for covered health care providers to make a good faith effort to obtain individuals written acknowledgment of receipt of providers Notice of Privacy Practices. The stated aim of this potential change is to reduce burden and free up resources for covered entities to devote to coordinated care. More than 100 U.S. Senators and House members weighed-in against the FTCs original proposal. And now, since the May 2019 release of the Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rule Making, more than 25 U.S. Senators have registered their continued concern with the Commissions proposed new requirements, stating that the FTCs reaffirmation of a prescription release confirmation proposal is both unnecessary and overly burdensome. According to the FTCs own data, few complaints regarding prescription release have been received and the Commission estimates that this new mandate would add millions in new regulatory compliance costs. It is especially troubling that the Commissions stated intent is to gain new investigative authority to target small and mid-sized independent medical practices serving communities in our state and across the country. As I understand it, the purpose of the ten-year review of the Contact Lens Rule is to assess its effectiveness based on a thorough, fact-based analysis and a process free of bias, false claims and insider-influenced policy. Doctors, like me, and our patients across the United States who are continuing to live and work under your agencys threat of baseless and punishing regulations look forward to participating in open and thoughtful discussions, including through the meetings we have been seeking with you and your fellow commissioners. Rick McManus, O.D.

comment: The commission should move forward with the modification of its proposal to amend the Contact Lens Rule. The modification will help inform more consumers that they do not have to purchase contact lenses from their prescribers. More consumers will become aware of the option to buy contact lenses from other retailers. In the past, I had to request my prescription because it was not given to me at the time of the fitting. I was able to buy contact lenses from a different seller at a cheaper price. I recently asked a friend if they received their prescription at their contact lens fitting and their response was you have to ask for it. She was not aware that prescribers are required by federal law to release a copy of the prescription regardless if the patient asked for a copy or not. Allowing automatic release of contact lens prescriptions will notify many more consumers of their right to have a copy of their contact lens prescription. This will help increase competition in the market and consumers will be encouraged to learn about other contact lens sellers. Prescribers should also verify prescriptions in the time allotted so that consumers can purchase contact lenses without delay. I agree that sellers can be viewed as altering a prescription if their verification request is made for a manufacturer of contact lenses that is not stated in the prescription. This will encourage sellers to only sell contact lenses that were specifically prescribed for the consumer. Overall, the modification of the Contact Lens Rule will benefit consumers and promote competition in the contact lenses market.

comment: I am writing to share with the Federal Trade Commission a report on big data that I recently submitted to the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) on behalf of Google LLC (Google). Although it was prepared in response to concerns raised by the ACCC, the report discusses in detail a number of subjects that have also been raised during the FTCs recent Hearings on Competition and Consumer Protection in the 21st Century, particularly regarding the role of data in digital platform competition and the conditions under which the utilization of data might create barriers to entry and expansion. It is my hope that the enclosed report will be helpful to the FTC in considering these important issues. My report was occasioned by questions raised in the ACCCs ongoing Digital Platforms Inquiry. In the context of that inquiry, the ACCC asked commenters for their views on whether data-driven network effects and economies of scale may give established digital platforms that possess large amounts of data an enduring competitive advantage. With regard to Google, the ACCCs Preliminary Report explored whether Google is insulated from dynamic competition by barriers to entry and expansion for search platforms... arising from network effects, including network effects that supposedly flow from the collection and utilization of user data. The ACCC explored whether Facebook is insulated from dynamic competition for similar reasons. As I explain in my report, I believe the answer to these questions is no. In my view, neither network effects nor the collection and utilization of user data prevent entry or competition from search rivals. With respect to network effects, search services are typically not characterized by either same-side or cross-side network effects. And, with regard to data, there is no economic evidence indicating that access to a large volume of user data is necessary to compete effectively. I describe the evidence supporting these conclusions in the attached letter.

comment: The power of collaboration in medicine has been an area of focused advocacy throughout my career. With particular regard to my tenure at Ballad Health, I have been an active participant in the development of this kind of collaboration between the health system and employed and independent physicians, and the critical good it can do for communities and patient populations. This is especially true in the region that Ballad Health serves, which is among the worst in the nation for several health-related challenges. As a testament to these beliefs in action, I currently serve both as chair of Ballad Healths Hospitalist Division, and chair of the systems Clinical Council. The Council provides oversight of the Medical Staff Committees of all 21 hospitals across Ballad Healths regional service area. In cooperation with the state of Tennessee and the Commonwealth of Virginia, this work has helped establish common quality standards, credentialing and peer review processes, and best practice requirements across the continuum of care. Through these efforts we were able to demonstrate improvement in 14 out of 17 key quality measures outlined in the COPA during our first year of operation as Ballad Health. In a state and region that has been ravaged by hospital closures and declining access to care for a decade or more, we are building a health system that can sustain itself through economic peaks and valleys, while addressing the devastating effects of obesity, diabetes, opioid and tobacco abuse, and mental health crises on the communities we serve. By standardizing care across disciplines and practices, leveraging shared data and benchmarking best practices, I strongly believe Ballad Health can best meet the most pressing challenges the region is facing and serve the communitys healthcare needs for decades to come. Best regards, Amit Vashist, MD, MBA, CPE, CACP, FAPA, SFHM, FACHE

comment: Dear Chairman Simons, I am an optometry student at the Arizona College of Optometry. For more than two years, the profession that I have chosen to enter has faced the threat of a seriously flawed Federal Trade Commission (FTC) plan to impose massive new costs and far-reaching new requirements on all contact lens prescribing. The proposal, even in its latest form, will divert precious resources away from the care and innovation and cast public doubt on the integrity of optometrists and ophthalmologists, para-professional staff and other employees. It should be withdrawn once again, and re-worked to put the interests of patients, doctors, and public health and safety first. The agencys own records and data clearly demonstrate that eye doctors across the country, in overwhelming numbers, comply fully with the prescription release requirements of the 2003 Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act. Instead of creating new burdens from Washington, DC impacting tens of thousands of doctors and millions of patients, please commit to a program of basic enforcement focused on outliers shown to be violating the law. Its especially notable that the FTCs actions remain at odds with the policy direction being pursued by Congress and Federal agencies to prioritize the elimination of burdensome, costly and unjustified mandates in health care, especially those that are overwhelming small and mid-sized health practices on the frontlines of care. Here are active examples that I hope the agency is aware of: -Merit Based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) Special Considerations for Small Practices: The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) developed the framework for MIPS acknowledging the regulatory burden that health care providers already are facing. Considering that reality, CMS reduced the number of clinicians that are required to participate. CMS supported this effort out of the agencys desire to give physicians more time with their patients, not computers. Additionally, CMS is mindful of the unique challenges that face smaller physician practices and added new bonus points for clinicians caring for patients in those settings. -Patients over Paperwork: CMS initiated this regulatory review in 2017 aimed at removing regulatory obstacles that get in the way of providers spending time with patients. -Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA): Currently, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) is considering eliminating or modifying the requirement for covered health care providers to make a good faith effort to obtain individuals written acknowledgment of receipt of providers Notice of Privacy Practices. The stated aim of this potential change is to reduce burden and free up resources for covered entities to devote to coordinated care. More than 100 U.S. Senators and House members weighed-in against the FTCs original proposal. And now, since the May 2019 release of the Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rule Making, more than 25 U.S. Senators have registered their continued concern with the Commissions proposed new requirements, stating that the FTCs reaffirmation of a prescription release confirmation proposal is both unnecessary and overly burdensome. According to the FTCs own data, few complaints regarding prescription release have been received and the Commission estimates that this new mandate would add millions in new regulatory compliance costs. It is especially troubling that the Commissions stated intent is to gain new investigative authority to target small and mid-sized independent medical practices serving communities in our state and across the country. I encourage the Commission to please enforce the law and regulations currently in place and to do more to protect the patients that I am committing my career to. Sincerely, Brittany Caputo

comment: Loot boxes and related "gacha" mechanics are incredibly dangerous when allowed to proliferate without any concern for who will be playing the games they are utilized in. Even individuals who are not particularly susceptible to the endorphin rush from them can tell you how effective they are, and how they can drive the most vulnerable to make massive purchases in attempts to get the items or characters they desire. While many companies argue that loot boxes are not gambling because nothing monetary is being risked (their argument being that you do not "own" any of the resulting digital items), the fact remains that they are psychologically indistinguishable from gambling even if they skate by on this technicality. While I do not think that paid loot boxes should be illegal, it is my belief as someone who has extensive experience playing these games that their inclusion represents a tangible danger to children and others who are particularly susceptible to gambling addiction. At the very least, the inclusion of paid loot boxes or gachas should warrant a warning label and an age rating not less than 18.

comment: As a practicing ophthalmologist, I am deeply concerned about proposals included in the Federal Trade Commission's proposed amendments to the Contact Lens Rule. While I would welcome changes to the Contact Lens Rule that prioritize patient safety, the prescription-receipt verification process and three-year record hold places an unfair burden on ophthalmology practices. This new burden is also unwarranted, as there is little evidence that ophthalmologists are not in compliance with the existing Contact Lens Rules. Most of my patients desire to purchase their contact lenses through our office for convenience and because of our competitive prices. They would rather not have a copy of their prescription as they know we have it readily available for them at anytime. Anyone who would like a prescription for their contacts is provided a copy with no hassle to them. To be required to give everyone a copy of something that most don't desire and then keep records that we did so for three years serves no positive purpose. It would put undue financial and administrative burdens on my office. I strongly urge the FTC to withdraw its latest proposed changes to the Contact Lens Rule and focus on efforts to enhance patient safety. Thank you for your consideration.
